# Today: the high-speed train and the ordinary flight

Today London is two and a quarter hours from Paris by train, closer in time than Lille was in 1850. Almost every city on Earth lies within a day. Yet for the longest journeys, the clock has barely moved since the 1970s: what has changed is not speed but price, frequency, and the sheer number of people travelling.

## A traveller: the first Eurostar passengers, 1994

On Monday 14 November 1994, the first fare-paying passengers travelled through the Channel Tunnel from London to Paris and Brussels, reaching both capitals in about three hours [@first-passengers-go]. The train pulled into the Gare du Nord a few minutes early; most of the passengers had booked their seats years in advance [@first-passengers-go]. A standard-class ticket cost £95 booked two weeks ahead (about $330 today) or £155 for a flexible fare (about $530) [@first-passengers-go; @100-1990-2026; @gbp-usd-historical].

The 50 km tunnel had taken six years and £10 billion to build [@first-passengers-go]. In 1994 the 790-seat trains reached 288 km/h in France but were held to 160 km/h on the old tracks of south-east England [@first-passengers-go]. Once a dedicated high-speed line to London was completed, the journey from St Pancras to the Gare du Nord fell to 2 hours 15 minutes [@high-speed-1]. A journey that took four or five days around 1800, and seven and a half hours by the boat trains of the 1890s, now takes about as long as a feature film.

## The maps

![Europe from Paris today](/maps/output/europe_today.png){#fig-europe-today fig-alt="Map of Europe with France and its neighbours almost all within six hours of Paris; Moscow, reached only with a connection, stands out as slower" aria-describedby="desc-europe-today"}

::: {#desc-europe-today}
France and its neighbours now fall almost entirely within six hours, much of it within three by high-speed train. The slowest parts of the European map are no longer the far edges of the continent but places without a direct flight: Moscow, a single flight of about five and a half hours in 1975, takes 10 to 13 hours door to door with a connection [@aller-russie-depuis].
:::

![The world from Paris today](/maps/output/world_today.png){#fig-world-today fig-alt="World map with major cities within a day of Paris: New York ten hours, Tokyo sixteen, Sydney about a day; remote interiors take two to five days" aria-describedby="desc-world-today"}

::: {#desc-world-today}
The world map is almost uniformly warm. New York lies about ten hours away, Tokyo and Hong Kong about fifteen or sixteen, Sydney about a day. Compared with 1975, the colours have barely shifted: long-haul jets fly at much the same speed as fifty years ago.
:::

## Travel times from Paris today

| Destination | Fastest journey | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lille | about 1 hour | Estimate, by TGV |
| Brussels | about 1½ hours | Estimate, by high-speed train |
| Lyon | about 2 hours | Estimate, by TGV |
| London | 2 hours 15 minutes | Eurostar timetable [@high-speed-1] |
| Rome, Madrid, Berlin | about 4 hours | Estimates, by air |
| Cairo | about 6 hours | Estimate |
| New York | about 10 hours | Estimate, by air |
| Mumbai | about 11½ hours | Estimate |
| Moscow | about 12 hours | 10–13 hours door to door with a connection [@aller-russie-depuis] |
| Tokyo | about 16 hours | Estimate |
| Sydney | about 24 hours | Estimate, with one connection |

## Conditions on the road

The experience of speed has split in two. Within Europe, the high-speed train runs from city centre to city centre. Between continents, travel is by jet at speeds little changed since the 1970s; supersonic travel ended with Concorde's retirement in 2003 [@air-france-commemorates].

## The effort of the journey

Most of the old effort now fits in a pocket. Airline e-tickets were devised in about 1994, and have been mandatory for members of the International Air Transport Association since 1 June 2008 [@electronic-ticket]. The suitcase stood up: Robert Plath's upright Rollaboard of 1987 superseded Sadow's flat wheeled case [@suitcase]. Within the European Economic Area, mobile roaming charges were abolished on 15 June 2017 [@european-union-roaming], so a traveller from Paris can call home from Lisbon or Helsinki at French prices.

What no ticket can shorten is jet lag, the one effort of the journey that speed has made worse (see the interlude on time).

## Paying the way

For most journeys from Paris, paying has become almost invisible: a card or a phone works nearly everywhere, and within the euro area there is no currency to exchange at all.

## Papers

On 14 June 1985, five countries (Belgium, France, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and West Germany) signed an agreement on the gradual abolition of their common border controls aboard the riverboat *Princesse Marie-Astrid*, on the Moselle near Schengen, where France, Germany, and Luxembourg meet [@schengen-agreement]. It came into force for some of them in 1995, and the Schengen Area, with no internal border controls, has since grown well beyond the original five [@schengen-agreement].

Britain stayed out, and Eurostar carries the border with it. At first French police checked passengers' documents on board; from June 1998 control booths were set up at the Gare du Nord [@juxtaposed-controls], and passengers now leave the Schengen Area and enter the United Kingdom before boarding [@juxtaposed-controls], arriving in Britain, for legal purposes, while still in Paris.

Further afield, a French visitor to New York needs no visa, but an online ESTA authorization, valid for up to two years [@visa-waiver-program].

One medical paper survives from the old sanitary conventions: the International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis, known as the yellow card or *carte jaune* [@icvp]. The International Health Regulations of 1969 required it to be printed in English and French, and its association with the colour yellow owes much to yellow fever, a vaccination commonly required for travel [@icvp].

## Risks

Travel has never been safer. Airline travel is now the safest form of transport; in the words of the National Air and Space Museum, 'it is far safer to fly than it is to get to the airport' [@evolution-commercial-flying]. The rare crashes, such as the Concorde accident of 25 July 2000, are remembered precisely because they are so rare [@evolution-commercial-flying; @air-france-commemorates].

## Who travels, and how many

Numbers have exploded. In 2025 there were nearly five billion passenger journeys by air, on nearly 40 million flights [@annual-review]. Paris's two main airports alone handled more than 100 million passengers in 2025: about 72 million at Charles de Gaulle and 35 million at Orly [@december-full-year; @orly-airport]. Where about 140 vehicles a day passed on the new roads outside Paris in 1788, and a few dozen passengers braved a winter Atlantic crossing in 1850, travel is now a routine part of ordinary lives. Crossing the road calls for rather more care than it did.
